source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources or paraphrases of them (see each document's sourcing note)

books.section: A. Colonial Resistance to British Policies in the Aftermath of the French and Indian War
The Sugar Act, the Currency Act, and the Stamp Act

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which British taxation policies changed the relationship between Britain and its American colonies, 1763–1774.

documents.title: The Sugar Act
documents.source: Sugar Act (American Duties Act), 1764, title and preamble. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The act's own stated purpose — raising revenue to pay for defending the colonies — which was new: earlier duties had been meant to regulate trade.
documents.text: An act for granting certain duties in the British colonies and plantations in America... for defraying the expenses of defending, protecting, and securing the same.

documents.title: The Stamp Act
documents.sourcing: The preamble states the tax's purpose in the act's own words: revenue for colonial defense, collected directly from colonists.
documents.text: An act for granting and applying certain stamp duties... towards further defraying the expenses of defending, protecting, and securing the British colonies and plantations in America.

documents.title: The Stamp Act Congress declares its rights
documents.source: Declaration of Rights and Grievances, Stamp Act Congress, October 1765. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Nine colonies speaking together for the first time, stating the constitutional principle behind their objection.
documents.text: That the only representatives of the people of these colonies, are persons chosen therein by themselves; and that no taxes ever have been, or can be constitutionally imposed on them, but by their respective legislatures.

documents.title: Dickinson on taxes
documents.source: John Dickinson, Letters from a Farmer in Pennsylvania, Letter II, 1767. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Dickinson, the colonies' most widely read pamphleteer, drawing the line between acceptable duties and unacceptable revenue taxes.
documents.text: If they have a right to levy a tax of one penny upon us, they have a right to levy a million upon us.

documents.title: The Massachusetts Circular Letter
documents.source: Massachusetts Circular Letter, February 1768, drafted by Samuel Adams. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Adams writing to the other assemblies, urging them to act together against the Townshend duties; London answered by ordering the letter withdrawn.
documents.text: That what a man has honestly acquired is absolutely his own; and he may freely give it away, but it cannot be taken from him without his consent.

documents.title: Revere's Bloody Massacre
documents.source: Paul Revere, The Bloody Massacre perpetrated in King-Street Boston on March 5th 1770. Public domain; image from the shared image pool.
documents.sourcing: A Patriot engraving printed weeks after the shooting: it shows an ordered volley, though the soldiers in fact fired in confusion. It shows how Patriots framed the crisis, not what the soldiers did.

documents.title: The First Continental Congress: the Continental Association
documents.source: Continental Association, adopted by the First Continental Congress, October 1774. Paraphrased.
documents.sourcing: Twelve colonies acting as one body for the first time, answering the Coercive Acts with a shared economic weapon and committees to enforce it.
documents.text: The Congress resolved that the colonies would stop importing British goods, stop exporting to Britain, and stop consuming British goods, and that committees in every town would see the agreement kept.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which British taxation policies changed the British-colonial relationship, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as salutary neglect before 1763, when Parliament left colonial taxation to the assemblies, or the war debt that pushed London to seek colonial revenue.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument about change or continuity.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without describing what they show, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument, with the evidence accurately described and tied to the claim.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the repeal of the Stamp Act in 1766, the Declaratory Act, or the Boston Tea Party and the Coercive Acts.
rubric.notEarned: A general statement with no specific example beyond the documents does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document's author, purpose, audience, or historical situation to the argument, for at least two documents, such as the Stamp Act preamble stating its revenue purpose, or Revere's engraving as Patriot propaganda.
rubric.notEarned: Identifying an author without explaining why it matters, or sourcing only one document, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the extent of change, showing that the relationship changed in stages rather than all at once, or weighing change against the loyalty colonists still professed in 1774.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: British taxation policies changed the relationship profoundly: before 1763 the colonies taxed themselves under assemblies London mostly left alone, but after the war Parliament claimed the right to tax them directly, and by 1774 the colonies were answering as a single body — though they still professed loyalty to the king.
Context: Before 1763 Parliament regulated imperial trade but left taxation to the colonial assemblies, a practice later called salutary neglect; the Seven Years' War left Britain about £133 million in debt and London decided the colonies should help pay for their own defense.
Evidence: Documents 1-2 show the new policy in London's own words — the Sugar and Stamp Acts were written to raise revenue for defense. Documents 3-5 show the colonial answer — the Stamp Act Congress, Dickinson, and the Circular Letter all asserting that only their own assemblies could tax them. Documents 6-7 show the break widening — Revere's engraving turning a street confrontation into a symbol of British cruelty, and the Continental Association organizing twelve colonies into one economic front.
Beyond the documents: The Stamp Act was repealed in 1766, but Parliament passed the Declaratory Act claiming the right to tax "in all cases whatsoever"; the Tea Act and the Boston Tea Party then brought the Coercive Acts, which closed Boston's port and rewrote Massachusetts' government.
Sourcing: The Stamp Act preamble states its revenue purpose openly, so it shows London's intent, not just its effect; Revere's engraving is Patriot propaganda printed to shape opinion, so it proves how the crisis was framed, not what happened in King Street; the Association is a public pledge, meant to be read by Britain as much as by the colonies.
Complexity: Change came in stages, not in a single break — each tax produced a colonial answer, each answer produced a British reply, and the relationship was remade step by step; and even in 1774 the Congress petitioned the king rather than declaring independence, so the old loyalty and the new defiance existed side by side.
